 Despite a matchup with the Arizona Cardinals, Matthew Stafford is ranked outside the top-12 at QB this week. Patrick Smith / Getty Images 
 By Andy Behrens Nov. 13, 2026 Updated Share article 3 It may feel as if the Los Angeles Rams are reeling, but they have actually won three straight games. It’s not as if everything is on fire. The Rams are headed into a friendly matchup on Sunday against the Arizona Cardinals, a team transitioning to its third quarterback in as many weeks. All-Pro defensive end Myles Garrett returned for L.A. last week as an absolute game-wrecker, delivering three sacks and a forced fumble. Head coach Sean McVay’s team is probably going to take a 6-4 record into the Week 11 bye.
 Advertisement
 And yet despite all the positive developments, it feels as if the Rams are slightly broken — not hopelessly broken, but moderately so.
 An offense that was treading water without star receiver Davante Adams (IR-hamstring) will definitely struggle after Puka Nacua suffered a multi-ligament knee injury (PCL/MCL) in last week’s win over Washington. Adams is expected to miss two more games , and Nacua won’t return for several weeks . Curiously, the Rams didn’t make a move for a receiver at the trade deadline, even as Indianapolis flipped veteran wideouts Keenan Allen and Josh Downs for modest returns.
 Los Angeles heads into the Arizona matchup with Konata Mumpfield, Tutu Atwell, Xavier Smith and sixth-round rookie C.J. Daniels as their presumptive top wide receivers. Those four players have combined for just 18 receptions this season. The Rams will also continue to use 13-personnel at an outlier rate , putting three tight ends on the field simultaneously.
 According to TruMedia, only 54.2% of Matthew Stafford’s passes have targeted a wide receiver this season, which ranks 24th among starting quarterbacks — and that was with Adams and Nacua involved. It seems entirely possible that L.A.’s wide receivers will merely serve as distractions over the next month, minimally involved and completely irrelevant in fantasy. Signing a post-injury veteran like Tyreek Hill or Odell Beckham Jr. (or Brandon Aiyuk when he becomes available) won’t alter the trajectory or tendencies of this team’s offense.
 We’re likely to see extreme usage for running backs Kyren Williams and Blake Corum, along with significant target totals for tight ends Tyler Higbee, Colby Parkinson and, if he ever gets healthy, Terrance Ferguson.
 If this sounds like a messy and suboptimal situation for Stafford … well, yeah. He’s buried at QB19 in Jake Ciely’s weekly ranks despite the appealing matchup. After L.A.’s bye in Week 11, the Rams will face a trio of frisky defenses: Green Bay, Kansas City and San Francisco. Stafford may not deserve serious starting consideration again in one-quarterback leagues until mid or late-December. It might feel strange to drop the reigning MVP from your fantasy squad, but he won’t be obviously playable anytime soon.
 Advertisement
 Forget the QB controversy, let’s discuss Cleveland’s backfield
 We have a segment of the fantasy community that would very much like to view Cleveland Browns running back Dylan Sampson as a player on the rise, if not an emerging star. The snap-share hawks are extremely fond of Sampson. He played 64.4% of Cleveland’s offensive snaps last week and 55.7% the week before, out-snapping teammate Quinshon Judkins in each game. Sampson certainly has some PPR appeal; he’s been targeted 13 times over the past two weeks. He’s also averaging 4.9 yards per carry, although he’s only run the ball 15 times this season.
 Let’s just be careful not to allow snaps to completely drive your decisions and assumptions about the roles of Sampson and Judkins. Here’s 44 seconds of Browns head coach Todd Monken describing the division of duties in his backfield , a clip in which he refers to Sampson as “our third-down back.” We are not currently in a situation in which one player has leapfrogged the other in terms of depth chart position. Cleveland’s offense, however, has an ongoing problem remaining on schedule, an issue for which Judkins definitely bears some responsibility.
 As Monken tells it, “The more you stay on track, the more you’re gonna see 10 [Judkins], and the more you’re not, and you’re in two-minute, the more you’re gonna see 22 [Sampson].”
 Cleveland’s running game ranks 30th in the league in yards before contact per rush attempt (0.69) per TruMedia, which you might be able to guess if you’ve been watching Judkins get hit in the backfield repeatedly. It’s not the healthiest rushing environment. Judkins pretty clearly will not be used as a volume receiver, so it’s more than fair to downgrade (or bench) him based on projected game flow. This week’s opponent, Houston, is a 4.5-point road favorite.
 If you’re looking for a ray of hope with Judkins, however, just take a glance at Cleveland’s rest-of-season schedule . It’s a series of neutral-to-favorable matchups, highlighted by a Championship Week date with Indianapolis. If you can somehow avoid the consolation bracket as a Judkins manager, he may prove useful in the money weeks.
 Advertisement
 Omar Cooper Jr. is quietly crushing
 Let’s just take a look at the year-to-date leaders in yards per route run, according to PFF:
 Jaxon Smith-Njigba, 3.49
 Mike Evans, 3.41
 Christian Watson, 2.98
 CeeDee Lamb, 2.91
 Zay Flowers, 2.90
 Puka Nacua, 2.86
 Omar Cooper Jr., 2.73 
 Tee Higgins, 2.71
 Drake London, 2.65
 Luther Burden III, 2.65
 One of those names is very much not like the others. Nine of those players are universally rostered in fantasy leagues — all of them early-round picks — and one is a rookie who’s likely still available to many of you. Cooper remains unattached in over one-third of leagues at the major platforms. He’s been excellent since returning from IR, a highlight machine who’s caught 19 balls for 276 yards and two scores over the past four weeks.
 Cooper isn’t yet challenging Garrett Wilson’s position atop the receiving hierarchy for the Jets, but he’s established himself as a near every-snap player. He’s certainly looking like a guy who deserved his first-round draft status back in April (and also looking like a guy the Rams maybe should have selected with the 13th overall pick). New York has a series of appealing matchups before its Week 13 bye (Buffalo Bills, Los Angeles Chargers, Miami Dolphins), so it’s a good time to be proactive with the rookie.
 Deebo Samuel expected to return at Dallas
 Under normal circumstances, we might suggest that you should not immediately insert a non-star into your lineup when they’re returning from a multi-week hamstring injury. But when Dallas is the opposing defense, it’s fine to be aggressive. San Francisco wide receiver Deebo Samuel was a limited participant in practice to open the week and is expected to return on Sunday . Mike Evans (Achilles tendinitis) is not quite ready to get back in the mix, but Samuel is obviously a significant weapon. He’s been sidelined since Week 5. Don’t be surprised if he makes noise in his return, given the quality of the matchup. Samuel has played five games this season and made three house calls.
 Travis Etienne’s return to practice could disrupt our Audric Estime plans
 There’s nothing quite like a date with the Carolina Panthers defense to get the old hamstrings feeling better — particularly if you’re a running back.
 New Orleans Saints RB Travis Etienne returned to practice on Wednesday after missing five games with a hamstring injury. The team won’t rush a decision on activating him for the upcoming matchup with Carolina, but it’s at least a possibility. This is yet another situation in which we’d want to be aggressive about starting a player in his return from injury, given the opponent. The Panthers have allowed the fifth-most rushing yards per game this season (133.4), the most rushing touchdowns (13) and the second-most fantasy points to opposing backs. If Etienne returns, we’re using him. And if he can’t, we’re firing up RB Audric Estime coming off his 72-yard, one-TD performance against Cleveland.
